questions.question: How does a cashback site make money to pay you?
options: It shares the commission retailers pay it when you buy via its link
questions.explanation: Retailers pay commission and the site passes part of it to you.

questions.question: To make sure cashback tracks, you should…
options: Click through from the cashback site and accept cookies
Buy through the retailer's app directly
questions.explanation: Tracking relies on cookies. Ad blockers and some extensions can break it.

questions.question: Using a voucher code that isn't listed on the cashback site can…
questions.explanation: Many retailers decline cashback when unauthorised codes are used.

questions.question: Cashback marked “pending” means…
options: The retailer hasn't confirmed it yet, which can take weeks
questions.explanation: Pending cashback can still be declined.

questions.question: Which of these commonly gets cashback declined?
questions.explanation: No sale, no commission, no cashback.

questions.question: A £400 laptop: 3% from a cashback site plus 1% from a cashback card. Total back?
Buy a £60 supermarket gift card at 5% back. You earn…
What's a sensible rule with gift card cashback apps?
options: Only buy for shops you'll definitely spend at, and spend it fairly soon
questions.explanation: Unused balances, or a retailer going bust, can lose you money.

questions.question: Why compare two cashback sites before buying?
options: Rates for the same shop can differ
questions.explanation: One site may pay double the other for the same retailer.

questions.question: Cashback is best treated as…
options: A bonus that's only real once it's paid out
questions.explanation: Don't spend it until it lands.

questions.question: Buying something you don't need just to get cashback…
options: Still costs more than not buying it
questions.explanation: 10% back on something you didn't need is still 90% spent.

questions.question: How do cashback sites earn money?
options: Retailers pay them commission for sending shoppers, and they share some with you
questions.explanation: Retailers pay affiliate commission; the cashback site shares part of it with you.

questions.question: Cashback usually pays out when?
options: After the retailer confirms the sale, which can take weeks to a few months
questions.explanation: Cashback is 'pending' until the retailer validates the transaction, often 30-90+ days.

questions.question: Your cashback shows as declined. Most common cause is:
options: The tracking was broken or the order didn't meet terms, like exclusions or returns
questions.explanation: Declines usually come from broken tracking, returns, gift cards at checkout, or terms exclusions.

questions.question: To maximise the chance cashback tracks, you should:
options: Add items from a different site
Click through from the cashback site, then complete the purchase in the same session without detours
questions.explanation: Start from the cashback link and buy in the same session; detours and blockers can break tracking.

questions.question: Cashback is best treated as:
options: Guaranteed income you can budget for
A bonus you only count once it's actually paid
A reason to buy things you don't need
questions.explanation: Never buy on the promise of cashback; treat it as a bonus on purchases you were making anyway.

questions.question: Which combination usually stacks best?
options: Cashback site + discount code from the retailer + loyalty points
Cashback site + a random code from an unofficial site, which may invalidate the sale
Two cashback sites for one order
questions.explanation: Retailer's own codes plus loyalty points usually stack with cashback, but always check the cashback terms.

questions.question: Why do cashback sites offer higher rates for buying gift cards?
options: They earn commission on card sales, and you then spend the card at the retailer
questions.explanation: Buying a retailer gift card through a cashback site can stack: a rate on the card plus the retailer's own loyalty on the spend.

questions.question: A risk of buying discounted gift cards from third parties is:
options: They may be void, stolen or revoked with no comeback
questions.explanation: Third-party cards can be invalid or clawed back; buy from trusted sources and treat big discounts as a warning.

questions.question: What should you check before signing up to a cashback site?
options: The payout minimum, how you get paid and the site's track record
questions.explanation: Check minimum payout, payout methods and reviews; reputable sites are free to join.

questions.question: Some banks or cards offer cashback automatically on all spending. The catch is usually:
options: You must keep a huge balance or it's only worth it if the account suits you
You pay tax on it always
questions.explanation: Built-in card cashback is real but small; it's only a win if the account or card fits your spending without fees.

questions.question: In-store cashback apps typically work by:
options: Linking your card so qualifying purchases trigger cashback automatically
You posting receipts to a depot
questions.explanation: Linked-card apps track purchases against offers automatically once your card is registered.

questions.question: Why can cashback on insurance or finance products be unreliable?
options: Tracking is trickier for long application processes and policies must often stay active a set time
questions.explanation: Finance cashback often requires a completed application and a policy held for months, so declines are common.

questions.question: What's the smartest way to use a sign-up cashback bonus?
options: Plan it around a purchase you were already going to make, meeting the minimum spend
Open ten accounts in one day
questions.explanation: Meet the minimum spend with real purchases you'd make anyway; don't spend to chase the bonus.

questions.question: Cashback earned through sites is usually paid:
options: In cash to your bank or PayPal, sometimes with a gift card bonus option
Only as shopping vouchers with no cash option
questions.explanation: Most sites pay to bank or PayPal, with gift cards sometimes paying a few percent more.

questions.question: You're about to make a big purchase. Best order of operations?
options: Check the cashback rate, any voucher codes and loyalty value first, then buy via the best stack
Buy on the most expensive site
Ask a friend to buy it for you
questions.explanation: A minute of checking before a big buy can add real money; after purchase, tracking is too late.

questions.question: Why do cashback rates vary between sites for the same shop?
options: Different affiliate deals and different shares of commission passed to you
questions.explanation: Sites negotiate different commission deals and keep different cuts, so compare before clicking.

questions.question: If a retailer you use often isn't listed on your cashback site, you can:
options: Check the other major cashback site, which may have different retailers
questions.explanation: Retailer coverage differs between cashback sites, so checking both is free money.

questions.question: Returning part of your order usually affects cashback how?
options: Cashback is only paid on kept items, or the whole order may be declined
questions.explanation: Returns void cashback on returned items and sometimes the whole tracked amount.

questions.question: What's a healthy attitude to cashback and reward apps?
options: Let them add value to purchases you already planned
questions.explanation: Cashback works for you when it follows your plan, not when it drives spending.

questions.question: Referral schemes on cashback sites typically pay you when?
options: When your referral signs up and earns or reaches a threshold
questions.explanation: Referral bonuses usually require the new user to actually earn cashback, not just sign up.

questions.question: You bought via a cashback link but nothing tracked. First move:
options: Wait a couple of days for tracking, then raise a missing-cashback claim with your receipt
questions.explanation: Tracking can lag; if still missing after the site's stated window, submit a claim with order details.

questions.question: Cashback sites are generally free to use because:
options: They keep a share of the retailer commission
questions.explanation: The business model is commission sharing; you should never pay to join a mainstream cashback site.
